Abstract
The high-level attention mechanism enhances object detection by focusing on important features and details, making it a 
potential tool for tumor segmentation. However, its effectiveness and efficiency in this context remain uncertain. This study 
aims to investigate the efficiency, feasibility and effectiveness of integrating a high-level attention mechanism into the U-Net 
and U-Net +  + model for improving tumor segmentation. Experiments were conducted using U-Net and U-Net +  + models 
augmented with high-level attention mechanisms to compare their performance. The proposed model incorporated high-level 
attention mechanisms in the encoder, decoder, and skip connections. Model training and validation were performed using T1, 
FLAIR, T2, and T1ce MR images from the BraTS2018 and BraTS2019 datasets. To further evaluate the model's effectiveness, 
testing was conducted on the UPenn-GBM dataset provided by the Center for Biomedical Image Computing and Analysis 
at the University of Pennsylvania. The segmentation accuracy of the high-level attention U-Net +  + was evaluated using the 
DICE score, achieving values of 88.68 (ET), 89.71 (TC), and 91.50 (WT) on the BraTS2019 dataset and 90.93 (ET), 92.79 
(TC), and 93.77 (WT) on the UPEEN-GBM dataset. The results demonstrate that U-Net +  + integrated with the high-level 
attention mechanism achieves higher accuracy in brain tumor segmentation compared to baseline models. Experiments con-
ducted on comparable and challenging datasets highlight the superior performance of the proposed approach. Furthermore, 
the proposed model exhibits promising potential for generalization to other datasets or use cases, making it a viable tool for 
broader medical imaging applications.

1  Introduction
The segmentation of brain tumours from normal brain 
tissues in medical images is a crucial step in diagnosing, 
treating, and monitoring patients with this condition [1–3]. 
Accurate segmentation helps doctors identify the exact loca-
tion and size of the tumor, assess its growth rate, and detect 
any abnormalities in the surrounding tissues [1, 4]. Better 
tumor delineation could be an application of brain tumor 
segmentation in Magnetic Resonance (MR) or Computed 
Tomography (CT) images for radiotherapy and/or surgical 
treatment planning [5–7]. Furthermore, segmentation plays 
a significant role in improving treatment outcomes for brain 
cancer patients [6, 7]. This approach enables researchers to 
analyse the data more efficiently and enhances the under-
standing of this debilitating disease [5, 6].
In recent years, the field of artificial intelligence (AI) 
has made remarkable strides, particularly in deep learning 
algorithms for brain tumour diagnosis [1]. These algorithms 
have undergone training on extensive datasets of medical 
images and have exhibited impressive results in identifying 
and segmenting brain cancer with exceptional accuracy [1, 
8, 9]. They employ intricate neural networks to differenti-
ate between cancerous and noncancerous tissue and accu-
rately classify the regions, which can significantly enhance 
the efficiency and precision of cancer diagnosis [10]. This

segmenting brain tumours in the context of Magnetic Reso-

that further improves the segmentation process [17]. The 
U-Net +  + model consists of a contracting path for captur-
ing high-level features and a symmetric path for recovering 
the spatial resolution of the input image [17]. Although the 
U-Net +  + model is complex and requires additional learn-

context information efficiently has proven to be advanta-
geous for accurately segmenting brain tumours [18]. In fact, 
one study found that the U-Net +  + model achieved a mean 
Dice similarity coefficient of approximately 0.9, which is 
considered to indicate high accuracy [19]. Additionally, the 
attention gate generates a soft region that is suggested to 
integrate into a U-shaped structure [20]. Other models, such 
as residual U-Net, use stacked residual modules to replace 
ordinary neural units as basic blocks, increasing the train-
ing time [21]. Combining low-level or high-level attention 
mechanisms increases deep learning's capacity to separate 
information storage from calculation [4]. In summary, the 
3D U-Net +  + model with residual modules and attention 
mechanisms could be a powerful and effective tool for seg-
menting brain tumours, and it has shown promising results.
The objective of this study is to assess the viability of 
implementing a high-level attention mechanism on U-Net 
for the purpose of optimising brain tumour segmentation 
performance. This contribution of this study provides the 
following insights:

mechanism module and a residual block to enhance fea-

and traditional U-Net to obtain comprehensive evalua-

2)	 The integration of an asymmetric high-level attention 
mechanism module into U-Net +  + represents a novel 
approach that can significantly improve image segmen-
tation performance. This module is capable of identify-
ing unusual patterns and understanding global context 
information without adding excessive computational 
complexity. This integration can potentially to enhance 
image segmentation capabilities without the need for 
substantial additional resources.
3)	 The HLNet extensive evaluations were conducted on two 
benchmark datasets, BraTS2018 and BraTS2019, and 
carried out alongside the independent UPENN-GBM 
clinically focused dataset. The experimental results of 
HLNet outperform prior brain tumor segmentation net-
works.
2  Related work
2.1  Literature review
U-Net +  + is an enhanced version of the renowned U-Net 
framework, which is extensively employed in tasks related 
to image segmentation [13, 17, 18]. It is known for its ability 
to produce highly accurate segmentation results by leverag-
ing deep learning techniques [17]. The U-Net +  + design 
encompasses a sequence of residual blocks, a neural network 
layer variant that enhances the performance by enabling it 
to assimilate more intricate representations of the input data 
[13, 18]. In the domain of brain tumor segmentation, UN-et 
+  + with residual blocks has been highly successful in pre-
cisely identifying and segmenting tumor regions from medi-
cal images [17].
In deep learning models, attention mechanisms are effec-
tively used to enhance their performance [22]. Pinpointing 
specific areas of the input sequence is crucial for generating 
the spatial output [23]. The mechanisms allow the model 
to assign weights to each part of the sequence according to 
its importance [4]. During model training, the model then 
pays closer attention to the more heavily weighted segments 
of the input sequence, leading to a better understanding of 
which areas are most significant for producing accurate and 
meaningful results [4, 22].
High-order attention mechanisms are a class of mod-
els that model and use complex and high-order statistics 
[24]. Using a high-order polynomial predictor, this method 
produces scale maps containing high-order convolutional 
activation statistics [24]. In contrast to first-order attention 
mechanisms, which enable models to focus on different seg-
ments of the input sequence based on their relevance to the 
current output, higher-order attention mechanisms allow 
models to attend to the sequence of attention weights of the 
data [25, 26]. The mechanism could simultaneously learn 
the object extraction on the input data by fusion [27]. The 
mechanisms capture subtle differences in the object and 
produce discriminative attention [24]. Obtaining object seg-
mentation from input data, particularly multidimensional 
objects, is important over time [25]. Higher-order atten-
tion mechanisms use the attention weights from previous

In Fig. 2, HLNet utilises the classic U-Net image con-
traction and expansion design, featuring an encoder on the 
left and a decoder on the right. The input image is 160 
× 160 × 4, with 160 × 160 pixels per image input and four 
channels. The encoder section incorporates five residual 
blocks as the fundamental network components, each con-
taining a residual connection and a dual convolutional layer. 
The flow diagram of residual block show in the Fig. 2. The 
residual block downsamples the input feature map via a 1 
× 1 convolution layer and then applies feature extraction 
and nonlinear transformation using a dual convolution 
layer. Batch normalisation is applied to hasten training 
and ensure model stability. Next, the residual connection 
is performed between the downsampled feature map and 
the map after feature extraction and nonlinear transforma-
tion, retaining the original input feature map information. 
Following the activation of the residual block, a maximum 
pooling operation is utilised to further reduce the spatial 
size and extract higher-level features from the feature map. 
The output of each residual block is the feature map after 
convolution and residual connection, with the input being 
the previous layer's output. The input image size is halved 
for each residual block, doubling the number of channels. 
During the decoder stage, feature fusion, upsampling, and 
splicing occur between the feature maps of each decoder 
stage. The feature extraction occurred on the spliced feature 
maps using the convolution module, which obtained fea-
ture-extracted maps. Furthermore, the high-level attention 
module is introduced by using a second-order calculation to 
enhance the performance. This module comprises multiple 
attention submodules that utilise convolution operations and 
sigmoid activation functions to generate attention weights, 
which are used to weigh different regions of the input fea-
ture maps. Finally, high-order feature fusion is executed 
on feature-extracted maps through the high-level attention 
module to yield the fused feature maps. The final stage of 
feature fusion combines different levels of feature infor-
mation through multilevel feature fusion with a high-level 
attention module. The feature maps eventually undergo 
corresponding convolution operations to obtain the final 
prediction results.

4  Materials and methods
4.1  Datasets
In this study, the BraTs2018 and BraTs2019 benchmark 
datasets were adopted to train and test the performance 
of the proposed model [30]. The BraTs2018 dataset con-
tains a total of 285 cases, including 210 cases of high-
grade glioma (HGG) and 75 cases of low-grade glioma 
(LGG). The BraTs2019 dataset included 49 HGG cases 
and 1 LGG case, which extends based on the BraTs2018 
dataset [30]. Moreover, the study evaluated the publicly 
available"University of Pennsylvania Glioblastoma Imag-
ing, Genomics, and Radiomics"(UPENN-GBM) dataset 
provided by the Center for Biomedical Image Computing 
and Analysis (CBICA) at the University of Pennsylvania 
[31]. The UPENN-GBM dataset contains 630 samples 
from patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, including T1, 
T1ce, FLAIR, and T2 [31]. The volume data for the four 
MRI sequences and ground truth set were acquired and 
obtained the dimension at 240 × 240 × 155 [30, 31].

Dice coefficient, Hausdorff distance, sensitivity, and positive

for binary classification tasks, and the level of agreement 
between the predicted results and the actual situation was 
measured. These three metrics have values ranging from 0 
to 1, with higher values indicating better model performance 
and lower values indicating poorer performance.

To ensure precise outcomes from the proposed deep 
learning network, a preprocessing technique is utilised to 
address inconsistencies in MRI volume intensity caused 
by motion artifacts, variability in acquisition sequences, 
and parameters. The data are normalised, and the inten-
sity values are reorganised to standardise the input MR 
image. A brain tumor mask is created using the surround-
ing background of the brain region. In addition, the brain 
images underwent skull removal if skull-removed brain 
images were unavailable, according to the UPENN-GBM 
database.
The preprocessing process in this study merged the four 
MRI images, which are T1, FLAIR, T2, and T1ce with the 
same dimensions. The dimension of the data was 240 × 240 
× 155 × 4. The data were then resized into 160 × 160 × 155 
× 4, which is half of the original size on x and y dimen-
sions. This reduces computational resource consumption and 
aligns well with the segmentation task. The ground truth 
data were also resized into 160 × 160 × 155 for comparing 
the segmented results.
During the training process, a randomised selection 
method was used to allocate 70% of the subjects to the 
training data, 20% to the validation data, and the remain-
ing 10% to the testing data. The BraTS2018 training dataset 
consists of 285 subjects with four MRI sequences (T1, T1ce, 
FLAIR, and T2) and an associated tumor label image. Addi-
tionally, 50 new BraTS2019 samples were incorporated into 
BraTS2018 and allocated using the same ratio. The tumor 
labels included background (label 0), necrotic and non-
enhancing tumors (NET, label 1), edema (ED) (ED, label 
2), and postcontrast enhancing tumors (ET) (ET, label 4). 
The"enhancing tumour"(ET, label 4), the"tumour core"(TC, 
labels 1, 4), and the"whole tumour"region (WT, labels 1, 
2, 4) were commonly used in the validation process as 
ground truth standards. The ET, TC, and WT images could 
be essential for accurately determining clinically relevant 
Gross Tumor Volumes (GTVs) during treatment planning 
and diagnosis on tumor region identification by outlining 
the boundaries of edema, necrotic components, and tumor 
cell locations [35].
4.4  Implementation details
This experiment is based on the PyTorch 1.17 framework, 
which was written in Anaconda Python 3.7. The worksta-
tion PC used for training and prediction runs Windows 11 
with an Intel Xeon W- 2245 3.90 Hz CPU, an NVIDIA RTX 
A4000 32 GB GPU, and 1.0 TB of RAM. The Adam opti-
miser was used as the experimental parameters [36]. The 
hyperparameters with initial learning rate were set to 0.0001 
with an early stopping parameter of 100, and the attenuation 
coefficient was 0.0001 to achieve better results [37]. The 
loss function used a combination of a binary cross-entropy 
loss function and a Dice loss function [29]. The early stop-
ping method was used to test the validation dataset after 
each training epoch. Once the best results are obtained, the 
training automatically ends. If the result is better than the 
best result obtained before, the training model is saved. The 
early stopping parameter of the experiment is set to 50, and 
the momentum is set to 0.3. In this experiment, the batch 
size was 32, and the number of training times was set to 150

for integrating the module within the proposed model was 
determined through comparative analysis. The module has 
the potential to improve feature extraction and mapping in

after feature fusion on the encoder and skip connection, 
thereby improving the capacity to target specific areas. Fur-

tumour regions and more accurately identifies the broader 
extent of the tumour during the decoding stage. In this study, 
the second-order attention modules are also tested in the 
attention U-Net, which obtained better Dice rather than 
U-Net++. Although this study emphasises the use of high-
level attention modules U-Net++, not attention U-Net, the 
results show high-level attention modules could have the 
potential for U-Net model enhancement.
Current research into the integration of high-level atten-
tion modules is currently limited due to the complexity 
of defining first-order and second-order levels within 
intricate model structures. However, the proposed high-
level attention module presents a promising solution by 
modifying a single variable to distinguish these levels. 
Depending on the application, a first-order level could be 
beneficial for segmenting a single primary tumor. Second-
order attention modules can detect small lesions, such as 
subtle and limited contrast brain tumor regions, multiple 
brain tumors, or brain metastases. While the UPENN-
GBM dataset demonstrated success with small lesions, 
other scenarios may be less certain. Further testing and 
evaluation will be required to explore the performance of 
this proposed model fully.

using the Adam optimizer are summarized in Table 4. The 
proposed model demonstrates a significant improvement 
over the standard single U-Net model on DICE results. 
However, its performance is comparable to the combined 
Volumetric Convolutional Network (V-NET) [55] and 
U-Net model [8, 38–54], suggesting that the proposed 
model not only surpasses the single U-Net but also achieves 
competitive accuracy in segmentation tasks. Although the 
BraTS and UPenn-GBM datasets are focused on brain 
tumors, the performance of the proposed model suggests 
its potential applicability to other tumor types and regions 
in both MRI and CT segmentation. The clinical applica-
tions of the model are not restricted to MRI; it can also 
be extended to CT imaging. While CT images differ from 
MRI in terms of resolution and tissue characteristics, they 
are often acquired alongside contrast-enhanced CT images. 
This highlights the potential of the proposed model to 
achieve significant performance in CT-based brain tumor 
segmentation. However, the development of such applica-
tions would require a large and diverse dataset for effective 
training and validation.
The objective of this study was to improve the accu-
racy and efficiency of brain tumor segmentation models 
by exploring a range of goals and objectives. The proposed 
model has been evaluated on clinical data, which serves as a 
benchmark to compare its performance against experimental 
procedures and assess its practical application in real-world 
medical contexts. This study focused on the potential of 
high-level attention modules, which can be used to enhance 
the performance of deep learning models designed specifi-
cally for brain tumour localisation and delineation. By lever-
aging advanced machine learning techniques, the proposed 
model aims to provide accurate and reliable segmentation 
results, which can help clinicians make more informed deci-
sions on treatment planning regarding patient care [6]. Fur-
thermore, this study aimed to identify new opportunities for 
developing more effective and accurate tumour delineation 
tools for diagnostic and treatment strategies for brain tumour 
patients [1].
Training large datasets can be challenging and requires a 
significant amount of memory, which can impact the train-
ing time. For example, 3D magnetisation-prepared rapid 
gradient-echo (MP-RAGE) isotropic images were obtained. 
Compared with conventional MRI, isotropic datasets have 
more slices, which introduces large amounts of information 
that must be processed. As a result, training isotropic 3D 
datasets is more complex and computationally expensive. 
Once the model is trained, the testing phase can be relatively 
fast. However, it is important to note that testing can still 
be time-consuming for models requiring complex compu-
tations. Another crucial issue is overfitting, which occurs 
when a model is trained too well on the training data, lead-
ing to poor performance on new and unseen data. To prevent 
overfitting, it is essential to use evaluation tools to identify 
any issues with the model's performance, ensuring reliable 
predictions and decision-making. Further investigations are 
also exploring the potential of implementing this technol-
ogy in multimodal deep learning networks for self-supervised 
learning performance and applicability, leading to significant 
advancements in the field and expanded applications.
The potential applications of the proposed model extend 
beyond brain tumor segmentation, as it can be trained and 
implemented for tumor segmentation in other organs, such 
as the kidney and liver. Furthermore, the simplicity of the 
proposed model allows for seamless integration into MRI 
scanners or scanning consoles, enabling real-time segmen-
tation of images immediately after MRI acquisition. These 
results could play a crucial role in enhancing clinical diagno-
sis and treatment planning. Another potential investigation

6.1  Limitation
The limitation of the proposed model lies in its requirement 
for more datasets and extended training time due to the 
need for additional iterations. While U-Net achieves opti-
mal results in fewer than 20 iterations, the proposed model 
requires up to 20 iterations to produce the best outcomes, 
which increases the risk of overfitting. Addressing this 
issue cannot rely solely on the dropout method; additional 
techniques are necessary to minimize potential errors and 
enhance the model's robustness.
Despite these limitations, the proposed model demon-
strates potential for extension to tumor segmentation in other 
organs and regions. However, achieving optimal results in 
tumor segmentation requires the availability of significant 
and diverse datasets. Open-source datasets with ground truth 
images are predominantly focused on the brain region, with 
limited MRI datasets available for other anatomical areas. 
Therefore, further work is needed to develop and curate 
internal datasets within medical centers to train and refine 
the model for broader clinical applications.
7  Conclusion
This study presents a novel model of HLNet that incorpo-
rates a high-level attention module and residual connec-
tions. This innovative module employs multiple attention 
submodules to effectively capture high-order information 
on input feature maps, enhancing the ability of object 
detection and identifying important image features. The 
experimental findings demonstrate that HLNet outperforms 
U-Net, U-Net++, and attention U-Net with high-level atten-
tion modules regarding segmentation performance on the 
BraTs2018, BraTs2019, and UPENN-GBM datasets. The 
high-level attention module encompasses various calculation 
categories and may be particularly suitable for brain tumor 
segmentation.

Abstract: The high-level attention mechanism enhances object detection by focusing on important features and details, making it a potential tool for tumor segmentation. However, its effectiveness and efficiency in this context remain uncertain. This study aims to investigate the efficiency, feasibility and effectiveness of integrating a high-level attention mechanism into the U-Net and U-Net + + model for improving tumor segmentation. Experiments were conducted using U-Net and U-Net + + models augmented with high-level attention mechanisms to compare their performance. The proposed model incorporated high-level attention mechanisms in the encoder, decoder, and skip connections. Model training and validation were performed using T1, FLAIR, T2, and T1ce MR images from the BraTS2018 and BraTS2019 datasets. To further evaluate the model's effectiveness, testing was conducted on the UPenn-GBM dataset provided by the Center for Biomedical Image Computing and Analysis at the University of Pennsylvania. The segmentation accuracy of the high-level attention U-Net + + was evaluated using the DICE score, achieving values of 88.68 (ET), 89.71 (TC), and 91.50 (WT) on the BraTS2019 dataset and 90.93 (ET), 92.79 (TC), and 93.77 (WT) on the UPEEN-GBM dataset. The results demonstrate that U-Net + + integrated with the high-level attention mechanism achieves higher accuracy in brain tumor segmentation compared to baseline models. Experiments con- ducted on comparable and challenging datasets highlight the superior performance of the proposed approach. Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits promising potential for generalization to other datasets or use cases, making it a viable tool for broader medical imaging applications.
